title: Learning by sitting in with Black and white bands upstate
summary: Kmen learned by sitting in; no color bars upstate and Black musicians shared tricks freely.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: I never took lessons on the saxophone, the clarinet. I sometimes was afraid to take lessons. I didn't want to mess around trying to change my way of playing. As long as I was getting along, alright. Well, actually you learn an awful lot from the college you worked with. A kid in those days, I don't guess that this is ever, it's certainly not possible anymore, it may never be possible again in America, but you could go, you could draw a thirty mile radius, a thirty miles, a circle, a thirty mile radius around my town, and I dare say you could find a hundred bands, big and small. And all of them, there was a great deal of sitting in and everything, or just listening. Both were instructive, sitting in and listening. As far as my age, I had the same enthusiasm for music, and there were many, made a point of this. Never missed a band, never missed going wherever there was a band, or wherever you could sit in. And this is from the age of twelve? No, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, after you got a little, you had to have some competence. You had to, you can't just sit in and blow nothing. You can't sit in and blow something. But you learn an awful lot sitting in. And then of course up there, being no colored bars, I often wonder how much this just had to do with perhaps shifting the scene of vitality in jazz from New Orleans to Northern cities. And the fact that you could sit in, now I'm not saying that in those early days you had mixed bands playing, you understand, as an organized professional group. That wasn't done. But there was plenty of sitting in. No bars there at all. And if a dance hall had a Negro orchestra, all the white musicians in the world could come there and sit in and play with them. That created no problem at all. So that you got an interchange there. And the Negroes were very instructive about jazz as they were playing it. They didn't try to sit on any secrets, at least the ones I knew. They were glad to show you everything that they could show you. You can't just transfer the way you play, but you can show a person a lot of tricks. So we had an environment that was wonderfully instructive. And then when you started playing, as you played with better bands, there were musicians drifting into that area from New York and from Canada and from Boston and from all around. Sometimes musicians already there were musicians. I remember when I was fourteen or fifteen or sixteen, there were musicians that were in their forties and had been playing quite a long time. I remember one especially when I came down from Canada. And he played up there for a while with Jack Denny when Denny was still starting up in Montreal. But he had a health problem and come to this area for his health, but still played occasionally. And playing with musicians like that, you learn a lot just playing with them. Jack Denny, huh? Yeah, Jack Denny was one of the bands that got nationally popular through radio. He used to have a program from CKAC, Montreal, I can remember very well. And had no brass band at all, just saxes and accordion. Later when he came down and made it bigger in New York he added brass, but he was popular for quite a while, Jack Denny. As I remember one time he had a Whitman Sampler album.
